Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia

choking on the first feed · pass a tube before you order a picture · fistula type by abdominal gas · age at presentationDid it start with the first feed, and will a nasogastric tube pass?

Source vignette Pt – term newborn boy delivered at home, 3 hours old, who coughs and brings back his first breastfeed while milk and saliva pool in his mouth · Exam – coarse breath sounds, retractions, a soft systolic murmur, upper left sternal border · Q – best next step

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Drooling, choking and vomiting with the first feed plus a nasogastric tube that will not pass is esophageal atresia; a film showing the tube coiled in the upper chest confirms it.
  • Gas in the abdomen means a distal fistula, the common type at about 85%; a gasless abdomen means pure atresia.
  • Before repair: nothing by mouth and continuous pouch suction; screen for VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, limb) anomalies with an echocardiogram and renal US.
What it is

Esophageal atresia (EA): the upper esophagus ends in a blind pouch; most types also carry a tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF), a channel between trachea and esophagus.

Driver

The foregut fails to partition from the airway in the embryonic period, weeks 4 to 7.

Triggers

A congenital mesodermal defect; other malformations in up to 50%, about 20% meeting VACTERL criteria

non-modifiable

Chain

The upper esophagus ends blind

saliva and milk fill the pouch and spill into the larynx

drooling, coughing and choking with the first feed

a distal fistula lets crying force air into the stomach and acid reflux into the lungs

abdominal distension and aspiration pneumonia

Insights

The fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid, so polyhydramnios may be the prenatal clue; it is not specific, since many disorders cause it.

Cyanosis with feeds can be reflex laryngospasm guarding the airway, so together with drooling and choking it points to the esophagus, not the heart.

In uteropolyhydramnios
First feeddrooling, choking and vomiting
Late infancy or childhoodH-type fistula, usually found after aspiration pneumonia
2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingAction
Choking, drooling or cyanosis with the first feedHold oral feeds; the tube test (step 4) comes before any further feed.
Coarse breath sounds or crackles before repairKeep feeds held, with continuous upper pouch suction and acid suppression (step 7); aspiration pneumonia makes repair more hazardous and can defer it (step 6).
Abdominal distension with a distal fistulaGastrostomy to decompress the stomach if repair is deferred (step 6); air is forced through the fistula into the stomach.
3Differential
Neonatal choking, vomiting and distress, most tempting first
DiagnosisDecides it
Esophageal atresia (EA) with distal tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF)Frothy secretions and choking from the first feed, maternal polyhydramnios; tube will not pass
Pure esophageal atresiaSame feeding picture; gasless abdomen on the film
H-type fistulaThe tube reaches the stomach; cough with feeds for months, repeated pneumonia
Cyanosis and sweating with feeds; no excess secretions
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaScaphoid abdomen, bowel gas in the chest, bowel sounds over the left lung; severe distress from delivery
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiency; low lung volumes, ground-glass with air bronchograms
Bilious vomiting, Down syndrome, double bubble
Neonatal abstinence syndromeMaternal opioid use; typically starts at 24 hours or later, with hypertonia and irritability
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosisAge 3 to 6 weeks, nonbilious projectile vomiting, hungry after, olive mass
EpiglottitisDrooling and stridor with fever in a school-aged child; not a newborn disease
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Formula mixed with saliva in the mouthMilk filled a blind pouch and spilled backCheck whether a nasogastric tube passes.
Soft murmur at the upper left sternal borderA possible VACTERL heart lesion, not the cause of the chokingEchocardiogram after the tube and film, before repair.
Maternal polyhydramniosThe fetus could not swallow amniotic fluid; not specificAt birth, check whether a nasogastric tube passes when atresia is suspected.
Imperforate anus in a newbornVACTERL associationPass a nasogastric tube; echocardiogram and US of the other systems.
Pause point
Suspected fistula with a murmur Offered first: an echocardiogram or a barium study The heart is screened after the diagnosis, before repair → The bedside tube decides
5Diagnostic criteria
Type by tube and gas
FindingType
Tube coils; gas in the abdomenAtresia with a distal fistula (the common type, type C), about 85%
Tube coils; gasless abdomenPure atresia, no fistula
Tube passes; cough with feeds and recurrent pneumonia, usually found laterH-type fistula, no atresia
6Severity
Timing of repair
FindingMeaning
Stable infantRepair now (step 7)
Extreme prematurity, aspiration pneumonia or other major malformationsDefer repair; a gastrostomy decompresses the stomach so acid does not reflux into the lungs
Extremely long gap between the two endsThe ends cannot be joined directly; a replacement operation (step 7)
7Treatment
1

Before repairAtresia confirmed

Nothing by mouth, parenteral nutrition, continuous suction of the upper pouch, head elevated, acid suppression. In the neonatal intensive care unit the infant lies prone, head up 30 to 40 degrees, right side down.

2

StableCondition stable

Surgery: ligate the fistula and join the esophageal ends; primary anastomosis is possible in about 80%.

3

Long gapExtremely long gap (step 6)

Gastric transposition or colon interposition may be performed.

4

DeferredRepair deferred (step 6)

Gastrostomy tube to decompress the stomach until repair.

5

After repairAll infants

Acid suppression for reflux; fundoplication may be needed if medical treatment fails.

8Follow-up
After repair
ProblemDetail
Leak or stricture at the anastomosisThe most common acute complications
Feeding difficulty and dysphagiaPoor motility of the distal segment, in 80 to 90%
RefluxMore than 40%; acid suppression (step 7)
Practice
  1. 5 h old term girl, born after a pregnancy with polyhydramnios, drools frothy saliva, coughs and turns blue during her first bottle; crackles at both bases and a soft systolic murmur → Nasogastric tube placement → Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
  2. 2 h old term girl drooling frothy secretions who choked on her first feed; a nasogastric tube meets firm resistance and will not advance → Chest x-ray with the tube in place → A coiled tube confirms atresia; gas below the diaphragm means a distal fistula
  3. Term newborn girl, maternal polyhydramnios, drooling; the feeding tube coils in the upper chest on x-ray and the abdomen is completely gasless → Esophageal atresia without a fistula → No tracheal connection, so no air reaches the stomach
  4. 8 mo old boy with three right upper lobe pneumonias and coughing and choking with liquid feeds since birth; a feeding tube passes easily into the stomach → H-type tracheoesophageal fistula → Bronchoscopy or prone contrast esophagram
  5. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, before surgical repair → Echocardiogram and renal ultrasound → VACTERL association
  6. 4 wk old boy with a week of nonbilious projectile vomiting, hungry after each episode, ultrasound showing a thickened elongated pylorus, low chloride and high bicarbonate → IV fluids and electrolyte repletion → Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; pyloromyotomy once the alkalosis corrects
  7. Newborn girl with upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease, maternal polyhydramnios, bilious vomiting on day 1, abdominal x-ray with a double bubble and no distal gas → Nasogastric decompression and IV fluids → Duodenal atresia; repair after stabilization and an echocardiogram
  8. 30 wk preterm boy grunting and retracting at 1 h of life, x-ray with diffuse ground-glass opacities, air bronchograms and low lung volumes → Respiratory distress syndrome → continuous positive airway pressure, then surfactant if the oxygen requirement rises
  9. 36 h old girl, irritable and tremulous with a high-pitched cry, sneezing and feeding poorly; mother maintained on methadone → Swaddling, low stimulation and rooming-in → Neonatal abstinence syndrome; morphine only if nonpharmacologic care fails
  10. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, saturating 96% in room air, awaiting surgical repair → NPO, head elevated, continuous pouch suction → Keeps pooled saliva out of the lungs and gastric acid out of the fistula
Age at presentation Age at presentation narrows the differential. First feed: TEF (tracheoesophageal fistula) with EA (esophageal atresia). From delivery: diaphragmatic hernia; in a preterm infant, respiratory distress syndrome. 24 hours or later: neonatal abstinence. 3 to 6 weeks: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Late infancy or childhood: H-type fistula; inspiratory stridor in infancy is laryngomalacia.
Pearls Polyhydramnios in utero is the prenatal clue, because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid · The tube that will not pass makes the diagnosis; the film with the tube in place confirms it · The abdominal gas pattern shows the anatomic type without endoscopy · VACTERL screening after diagnosis: echocardiogram and renal US
Pairs with Posterior Urethral Valves covers the opposite amniotic fluid clue: too little fluid, because no fetal urine leaves the bladder, leading to Potter sequence. Cyanosis in the Newborn covers bilateral choanal atresia, the other newborn who turns blue with feeds; a catheter will not pass the nose, and crying turns the infant pink. Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers VACTERL beside CHARGE, trisomy 13 and DiGeorge syndrome, each told apart by the finding only it has.
Transferable rule When a newborn chokes or vomits with the first feed, first check whether a nasogastric tube reaches the stomach, before any imaging or drug. Imaging only confirms what the tube found.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpiglottitis is a febrile school-age disease; a 3-hour-old cannot have it.
Sequencing trapEchocardiography is indicated for VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) screening after the diagnosis, not before it.
True-fact-wrong-slotPyloric stenosis needs 3 to 6 weeks for the muscle to hypertrophy, and it gives projectile vomiting, not coughing with saliva-mixed formula at 3 hours.
True-fact-wrong-slotSurfactant treats respiratory distress syndrome in the preterm lung; this is a term newborn whose retractions come from aspirated secretions, which surfactant does not fix.
Salient decoyThe maternal drug history points at neonatal abstinence syndrome, but withdrawal typically begins at 24 hours or later, never pools saliva or causes coughing with feeds, and is treated first without drugs.
